1198.tomorrow: each as a lens for a week
1198.howItsDone: Nyaya and Vaisheshika are traditionally studied together, and students of Indian logic learn the Nyaya Sutra's means of knowing alongside Vaisheshika's categories of what there is.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday began each as a lens for a week: six schools, six questions, clicked in like lenses at the eye doctor.
screen: `SIX LENSES.` · `THE FIRST PAIR.`

segments.voice: Eight in the morning, at the bus stop. A neighbor leans over and says the bakery on the corner is closing for good. She heard it from her cousin. By lunch, it's all up and down the street. Later that afternoon, a friend snaps at you over something small, and a thought can stick for the rest of the day: so that's who they really are. Two ordinary moments. In both, something was taken as known a little too fast. Time for the first pair of lenses, the two schools that tradition studies together, Nyaya and Vaisheshika.
screen: `THE BAKERY IS CLOSING.` → `A FRIEND SNAPS.` → `KNOWN A LITTLE TOO FAST.`

segments.voice: First, the Nyaya lens. Its question: how do I know? The Nyaya Sutra names the means of right knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and the word of a reliable person. Click that lens onto the bus stop. Did anyone see a sign on the bakery's door? That would be perception. Is someone reasoning from empty shelves? That's inference, and Nyaya tests it. Or is it testimony? Then the question becomes whose. The Sutra says the word that counts is the word of a reliable person, someone who knows and tells it straight. A cousin of a neighbor, unchecked, isn't that yet. Under this lens, the rumor doesn't become false. It just becomes not yet known. Now the Vaisheshika lens. Its question: what is this made of? We met its list earlier in this part: substance, quality, action, and more. Click it onto your friend. There's the person, the substance. There's the irritation, a quality, passing through. There's the snapping, an action, a single movement that came and went. Vaisheshika keeps those apart on purpose. A quality lives in a thing; it isn't the thing. An action happens to a thing; it doesn't define it. So the thought, that's who they really are, turns out to be a category mistake. You took a quality for the substance. These two lenses are cool and patient. They slow down the leap. That's why tradition pairs them. One checks how you know. The other checks what you're looking at.
screen: `NYAYA: HOW DO I KNOW?` · `WHOSE WORD IS IT?` · `VAISHESHIKA: WHAT IS THIS MADE OF?` · `A MOOD IS NOT A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Let a recent impression of a person come to mind, and ask the Nyaya question first: did I see this, reason to it, or hear it from someone? Then the Vaisheshika question: is this the person, a quality passing through them, or one action that came and went, letting the person stay whole while the mood and the moment fall into their places. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the first pair: Nyaya asks how do I know, Vaisheshika asks what is this made of. Today's word.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, each as a lens for a week gave us the first pair: Nyaya asks how do I know, Vaisheshika asks what is this made of.
screen: `HOW DO I KNOW? WHAT IS IT MADE OF?` · `THE SECOND PAIR.`

segments.voice: The light turns green, and before the first car has even rolled, the horn behind it blares. Long and loud. The driver up front grips the wheel. Heat climbs into her face, her chest tightens, and a whole speech starts assembling itself in her head, all in a couple of seconds. She doesn't turn around. Her hands stay on the wheel. But inside, the car is on fire. Now the second pair of lenses, the two schools tradition studies side by side, Samkhya and Yoga, on that hot moment.
screen: `THE LIGHT TURNS GREEN.` → `A HORN, A HOT FACE.` → `INSIDE, THE CAR IS ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: First, the Samkhya lens. Its question: who is watching? We met its great division earlier in this part. On one side, prakriti, everything that moves and changes. On the other, purusha, the witness, who sees and never acts. Here's the surprise when you click it onto that intersection. The heat, the tight chest, even the speech, even the sense of I've been insulted, all of it sits on prakriti's side. In Samkhya, the I-maker is part of nature. So there's the storm, and there's the one seeing the storm, and the seeing isn't burning. Now the Yoga lens. Its question: what is the mind doing right now? The Yoga Sutra defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's movements. Then, it says, the seer rests in its own nature. Otherwise, the seer seems to take on the shape of whatever the mind is doing. That's the driver exactly: for a few seconds, she was the speech. So how do the movements settle? A few lines later the Sutra answers: by practice and by letting go. Practice is the steady effort to stay in that stillness. Letting go is loosening the thirst for things. Here, the need for the horn to stop and the speech to be delivered. Under this lens, the hot moment isn't a failure. It's where the practice happens. That's why tradition pairs these two. Samkhya draws the map: the seer and the seen. Yoga gives the steps for living on that map.
screen: `SAMKHYA: WHO IS WATCHING?` · `THE HEAT IS ON NATURE'S SIDE.` · `YOGA: WHAT IS THE MIND DOING?` · `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Let a recent sting come to mind, small is fine. With the Samkhya lens, notice that all of it, the heat, the story, the I that was hurt, is being seen, and rest a few breaths as the seeing; with the Yoga lens, come back to the breath, stay a little longer than is easy, and loosen your hold on how that moment should have gone. If you pray, you can offer the sting where you offer things.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the second pair: Samkhya asks who is watching, Yoga asks what the mind is doing. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each as a lens for a week. The heat is seen, and the seeing isn't burning. Go gently.

1200.title: each as a lens for a week
1200.word: each as a lens for a week

1200.howItsDone: Mimamsa and Vedanta are traditionally studied as the earlier and later inquiry, and some Hindus recite Bhagavad Gita 4.24, which speaks of the offering as Brahman, before a meal.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, each as a lens for a week brought the second pair: Samkhya asks who is watching, Yoga asks what the mind is doing.
screen: `WHO IS WATCHING? WHAT IS THE MIND DOING?` · `THE THIRD PAIR.`

segments.voice: It's ten at night. Dinner is over, everyone has drifted off, and the sink is full. Plates with sauce drying on them. A pot that needs soaking. The same sink as last night, and the night before. Nobody will see you do this. Nobody will thank you. And tomorrow it will be full again. If any moment in a day feels like it means nothing, it might be this one. So the last pair of lenses, the earlier inquiry and the later one, Mimamsa and Vedanta, come and stand at the sink.
screen: `TEN AT NIGHT. A FULL SINK.` → `NOBODY SEES, NOBODY THANKS.` → `FULL AGAIN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: First, the Mimamsa lens. Its question: what is this act for? We spent a week with this school. Mimamsa takes an act seriously in itself. Done rightly, in the right order, with care, an act isn't empty because it repeats. Tradition counts some rites as daily duties, done again and again, and the repeating is part of them. Click that lens onto the sink and the dishes stop being a chore in the way of your evening. They become an act with an order: soak, scrub, rinse, rack. Done with care, it is complete in itself. Now the Vedanta lens. Its question: what does all of it rest on? The Bhagavad Gita has a verse that holds both lenses at once. It uses the language of a fire offering, and says, in effect: the act of offering is Brahman, the offering is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act reaches Brahman. Some Hindus say this verse before eating. It keeps every piece of the ritual, the offering, the fire, the one who offers. Mimamsa would recognize all of it. And then it lets the Vedanta lens show what each piece rests on. Stand at the sink with both. The Mimamsa lens says: do this rightly, it matters as an act. The Vedanta lens says: look again at what is doing the washing, and what is being washed. The sink is the same. What it rests on comes into view.
screen: `MIMAMSA: WHAT IS THIS ACT FOR?` · `AN ORDERED ACT, COMPLETE IN ITSELF.` · `THE GITA: ALL OF IT IS BRAHMAN.` · `VEDANTA: WHAT DOES IT REST ON?`

segments.voice: See a single plate, and with the Mimamsa lens go through it in order: warm water, soap, scrub, rinse, rack. Then, with the Vedanta lens, ask quietly what the water, the hands and the one watching all rest on, and let the question soften the picture. If you pray, you can offer the plate and the hands to the One you pray to.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the third pair: Mimamsa asks what this act is for, Vedanta asks what it all rests on. Today's word.

1201.howItsDone: Traditional students of Indian philosophy learn the darshanas from their own root texts and commentaries, and classical scholars such as Vachaspati Mishra wrote commentaries on several schools, setting out each one's case in its own terms.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, each as a lens for a week brought the last pair: Mimamsa asks what this act is for, Vedanta asks what it rests on, and a Gita verse holds both.
screen: `THE LAST PAIR.` · `ALL SIX, ONE SHELF.`

segments.voice: There's a story people tell about a scholar named Vachaspati Mishra. He was writing a commentary, and he worked at it so long and so completely that he lost track of everything else, including the woman who kept the lamp lit beside him, his wife. When he finally looked up and asked who she was, she told him. Moved, so the story goes, he named the book after her: the Bhamati. The story may be legend. But the scholar's shelf is real, and it's strange. On the last day of this part, it shows how to hold all six darshanas at once.
screen: `A SCHOLAR BENT OVER HIS BOOK.` → `THE ONE WHO KEPT THE LAMP LIT.` → `A BOOK NAMED FOR HER.`

segments.voice: Here's what's strange about the shelf. The Bhamati is a Vedanta commentary, in Shankara's line. But Vachaspati Mishra is also remembered for commentaries on Nyaya, on Samkhya, on Yoga and on Mimamsa. Schools that argue with each other, sometimes sharply. And he wrote on each of them from the inside, carefully, laying out its case in its own terms. That's what a lens is. Not a team jersey. A way of seeing you learn well enough to look through. So here are all six, one last time. Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching? Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on? Each one, these weeks, brought something into focus that the others left soft. And now the title's invitation, plainly. Each as a lens for a week: a school a day, its question carried from morning until night, and a last day with no lens at all. It ends with no winner. That's the point of the part we're closing, schools of thought, never ranked. The tradition kept all six on one shelf, argued among them for a long time, and kept the lamp lit for the next reader. Tomorrow the lineage track picks up again, with a different teacher, Krishna speaking to his friend Uddhava in the Bhagavata, on action.
screen: `ONE SCHOLAR, MANY SCHOOLS.` · `A LENS, NOT A TEAM JERSEY.` · `ALL SIX QUESTIONS.` · `A DAY FOR EACH LENS.`

segments.voice: Picture the first ordinary thing you'll do tomorrow morning, filling a kettle, finding your keys, opening a door, and let whichever of the six questions arrives first stand in front of it. Look through it for a few breaths and notice what comes into focus, then set the lens down and rest in the plain scene without any question at all. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.

1202.title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
1202.hook: Krishna is about to leave the world, and his friend asks for one thing: take me with you
1202.howItsDone: Students of the Bhagavata Purana read the eleventh book's long dialogue between Krishna and Uddhava, known as the Uddhava Gita, as a teaching in its own right, and it is recited along with the rest of the Purana when the whole text is read aloud.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Last week, each as a lens for a week: six schools, six ways of seeing, and none of them ranked. Now the lineage track comes back, on the path of action.
screen: `SIX LENSES, NONE RANKED.` · `NOW, THE PATH OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Krishna is about to leave the world. In the Bhagavata's eleventh book, the gods come to remind him that his work on earth is done, and his own clan is heading toward its end. Uddhava hears it: his close friend, the learned messenger who once carried his words to Vraja. He comes to Krishna alone and asks for one thing: take me with you. He says he can't bear to be apart from him. What Krishna gives him instead is a long teaching. Tradition calls it the Uddhava Gita.
screen: `KRISHNA IS ABOUT TO LEAVE.` → `TAKE ME WITH YOU.` → `WHAT HE GETS INSTEAD: A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Krishna's first answer sounds hard. Don't follow me, he says. When I'm gone, let go of your attachment to family and friends, fix your mind on me, and wander the earth seeing everything evenly. Uddhava doesn't pretend. In effect he says: this kind of letting go is hard for people like me, whose minds cling to the body and to what is ours. Teach me how. And Krishna does, chapter after chapter, before he goes. That's the shape of the whole Uddhava Gita: an honest question, and a teacher who stays to answer it. Why read it on the path of action? Back on day seven, karma meant action itself, not payback. And Uddhava isn't a sage in a cave. He's a man with duties, a household, a city, and a friend about to be gone. His question is the karma question: how do I keep acting in a world that keeps losing things? The next few days come at it from several sides: what to learn from the people who wrong you, which path suits whom, where joy and sorrow really come from, and how to work without hurry. And notice: Krishna doesn't take Uddhava with him. The teacher leaves, and the student keeps living. Karma, in this book, starts right there: with the work a person does after the one they leaned on is gone.
screen: `DON'T FOLLOW ME. LET GO, AND WANDER.` · `THIS IS HARD FOR ME. TEACH ME HOW.` · `THE KARMA QUESTION: HOW DO I KEEP ACTING?` · `THE TEACHER LEAVES; THE STUDENT LIVES ON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something and isn't here to ask anymore, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who moved away, and instead of reaching for the loss, reach for one thing they left you: a habit, a saying, a way of doing an ordinary job. Hold that one thing, and if you pray, offer that person and that gift to the One you pray to. If a loss feels too heavy to hold alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Karma. Action, work, the deed itself. In the Uddhava Gita it begins with one honest question: how to keep acting when the one you leaned on is leaving.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. What the teacher left is what you work with now. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1203.title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
1203.hook: a king meets a young wanderer with nothing, and asks where his calm comes from
1203.howItsDone: The avadhuta's list of teachers in the Bhagavata's eleventh book is a familiar teaching story among Hindus, and tradition identifies the avadhuta with Dattatreya, honored as a teacher of teachers.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma began with a goodbye: Uddhava asked to be taken along, and Krishna stayed to teach him instead.
screen: `TAKE ME WITH YOU.` · `A TEACHING INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: A king out in the world meets a young man who owns nothing. No house, no plans, no worry on his face. The king is Yadu, an ancestor of Krishna's own clan, and he can't help asking. You're clever and capable, he says, yet you live like a child, untroubled. People all around are burning with wanting, and you stand there cool, like an elephant in a river while the forest burns. Where does your calm come from? Krishna tells this story to Uddhava early in their dialogue. The wanderer is an avadhuta, one who lives outside the world's usual rules. His answer: I've had many teachers. And the first one is right under your feet.
screen: `A KING MEETS A WANDERER.` → `WHERE DOES YOUR CALM COME FROM?` → `I'VE HAD MANY TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: The first teacher is the earth. In paraphrase, here's what the avadhuta learned from it: a steady person, even when pushed around by other beings, remembers that they too are moved by forces beyond their control, and doesn't step off the path. People dig the earth, plow it, build on it and walk on it all day. It doesn't shake anyone off. It keeps holding things up and growing food. This is karma from an unexpected side. Karma talk often starts with my actions and what comes back to me. The avadhuta turns it around. The other person, the one acting badly, is caught in a web of causes too. Not excused. Understood. Their action is theirs; my steadiness is mine. And the earth doesn't pretend nothing happened, or argue. It simply doesn't swerve. That isn't being a doormat. It's not letting someone else's bad day rewrite your path. After the earth, the avadhuta names many more teachers: the wind, the sky, water, fire, the moon, a python, a moth, a honeybee and others, each with its own lesson. Krishna tells the story so Uddhava can see the world itself as a classroom. But the list begins at the ground, with the teacher everybody stands on.
screen: `THE EARTH: PUSHED, AND STILL STEADY.` · `OTHERS ARE MOVED BY CAUSES TOO.` · `NOT A DOORMAT: JUST DON'T SWERVE.` · `THE WORLD AS A CLASSROOM.`

segments.voice: Feel what's holding you up, the chair, the floor, the earth under the building, and let your weight go into it. Bring to mind one person who pushed you lately with a sharp word or a careless move, and without replaying it, say to yourself: they were moved by things I can't see; then come back to the ground holding you. If you pray, you can hold that person before the One you pray to.
Karma. Action, and the web of causes behind it. From the earth the avadhuta learned that others are moved by causes too, and not to swerve.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. The ground takes every step and still holds. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1203 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA: THE BHAGAVATA'S UDDHAVA GITA.`

1204.title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
1204.hook: who is the path of action actually for? the Uddhava Gita answers: people who still want things
1204.howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of three paths, jnana, karma and bhakti, and some say a student's temperament and stage of life help decide which path to emphasize, drawing on teachings like this one in the Bhagavata's eleventh book.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's karma came from the ground: the earth gets pushed all day and doesn't swerve.
screen: `THE EARTH DOESN'T SWERVE.` · `WHO IS ACTION FOR?`

segments.voice: Who is the path of action actually for? Deep in the dialogue, Uddhava asks something close to it. The Vedas, he says in effect, tell people what to do and what not to do. They praise good works, and they also speak of a state beyond works altogether. So which is it? Do something, or stop doing? It sounds like a question that needs a side. Krishna doesn't pick one. He looks at the people asking, and sorts the paths by who's walking them.
screen: `DO SOMETHING, OR STOP DOING?` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T PICK A SIDE.` → `HE LOOKS AT THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Krishna says he has given three yogas, three paths, so people can reach the good: jnana, the path of knowing; karma, the path of action; and bhakti, the path of devotion. Then the sorting. Jnana suits those who have grown weary of action and turned away from it. Karma suits those who haven't, whose hearts still hold desires, who still want things from the world. And bhakti suits someone who, by some good fortune, has come to love hearing about him, neither fed up with the world nor tied too tightly to it. Sit with that middle line. The path of action isn't reserved for finished saints. It's for people with ambitions, a to-do list, a pull toward the world. The Uddhava Gita doesn't scold that wanting. It gives it a road. How long does a person stay on it? The very next verse answers: keep doing the work until you grow weary of it, or until faith in hearing his stories wakes up. Two ways off the road, and no deadline. For someone in the middle of a busy life, it's a quietly kind teaching. It doesn't say drop everything first, then you can begin. It says begin where your wanting already is.
screen: `THREE PATHS: KNOWING, ACTION, LOVE.` · `ACTION IS FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.` · `STAY UNTIL WEARY, OR UNTIL FAITH WAKES.` · `BEGIN WHERE YOUR WANTING IS.`

segments.voice: Without judging it, let one thing you want rise up, a result at work, a change at home, something you're building, and look at it clearly, the way you'd look at a road from the top of a hill. Then ask what one honest piece of work this wanting is asking of you. If you pray, you can offer that wanting, just as it is, to the One you pray to.
Karma. In the Uddhava Gita, the path of action: for hearts that still want things, walked until weariness comes or faith wakes up.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Work is the doorway for the one who still wants to work. Same time tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1204 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA: THE BHAGAVATA'S UDDHAVA GITA.`
